newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Semis - Get rates easing, power boost.
newsitem.headline: Australian Semis - Get rates easing, power boost.

text.p: *Semi yields were substantially lower on the week after the RBA's easing, more talk on prime asset ratio (PAR) arrangements and New South Wales mulling the sale of its power industry.

Semi-government bonds were finally turning slightly offered after rallying sharply last week, but yields were still substantially lower than a week ago, and the market once again outperformed Australian government debt.
This outperformance was despite a marked rally in government debt after the Reserve Bank unexpectedly cut official interest rates by 50 basis points to 5.50 percent on Friday.

The semis market continues to be supported by talk that the Reserve Bank will change the prime asset ratio (PAR) under its prudential supervison arrangements to include state bonds as Federal government debt supply declines.
At present banks have to hold 6.0 percent of their liabilities invested in Australian dollar assets in government securities or cash.

"Assuming the RBA retains some PAR requirement, then it is likely that inclusion of semi-government debt would receive consideration," said David Bassanese, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
"This would effectively open up a new market for semi-government debt and should lead to downward pressure on current semi spreads," he added.

Talk of this change has been in the market for some time, but gathered pace again after the Federal budget on May 13 when the government projected a negative borrowing requirements to the 2000/01 fiscal year.

And just when buying on this speculation was waning, the market got a further boost on Thursday from the announcement that the New South Wales state government is mulling a A$22 billion sell-off of the state's power industry.

"We saw a strong bid for TCorp (NSW Treasury Corp) bonds on Friday. It would effectively wipe out their debt, although it's going to be a few years in the making, and by then we could have a new government," one trader at a European bank in Sydney said.
Meanwhile, Queensland will be handing down its state budget on Tuesday, as will South Australia on Thursday.
